source.title: Are rolling averages a good way to assess training load for injury prevention?

paper.citation: Menaspà, P. (2017). Are rolling averages a good way to assess training load for injury prevention? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(7), 618–619. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096131
paper.abstract: Are rolling averages an adequate representation of training load when practitioners and researchers examine injury risk? Participants: None; this is correspondence, not an original study. Sport and level: General elite-sport load monitoring, with relevance to sports whose loads do not follow regular weekly patterns. Training or return-to-play context: Training-load modeling and injury-risk communication. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Conceptual critique supported by a fictitious example and selected references; no systematic evidence search or empirical validation. Design: Peer-reviewed correspondence/commentary. Exposure or intervention: None. Comparator: Rolling acute and chronic averages versus models that retain temporal patterning or decay. Measurements and outcomes: A constructed four-week load example for three fictitious athletes; no observed injuries or performance outcomes. Analysis: Conceptual argument; no statistical analysis.
paper.tldr: This correspondence states two enduring interpretive problems with rolling-average load summaries: they erase within-window variation and weight recent and older sessions equally. Three fictitious athletes can have identical last-week load of 50 AU, four-week average load of 35 AU, and acute:chronic ratio of 1.43 despite markedly different daily and weekly patterns. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Peer-reviewed correspondence/commentary. Exposure or intervention: None. Comparator: Rolling acute and chronic averages versus models that retain temporal patterning or decay. Measurements and outcomes: A constructed four-week load example for three fictitious athletes; no observed injuries or performance outcomes. Analysis: Conceptual argument; no statistical analysis.
paper.findings: Three fictitious athletes can have identical last-week load of 50 AU, four-week average load of 35 AU, and acute:chronic ratio of 1.43 despite markedly different daily and weekly patterns. The author argues that rolling averages obscure variation within the selected window. Rolling averages also treat a session from the previous day and one from four weeks earlier as equally influential, despite the time-varying effects of training stimuli. The proposed alternative—nonlinear training-load modeling—is explicitly a hypothesis requiring further sport- and individual-specific research.
paper.limitations: This letter provides no new athlete data and cannot estimate whether any alternative model predicts injury better. The example is deliberately fictitious and illustrates information loss, not causal injury mechanisms. Critiquing rolling averages does not validate training monotony, exponentially weighted averages, Banister-type models, or any other substitute. Association between a load metric and injury risk does not show that the metric causes injury or supports individual clinical decisions. Injury risk is multifactorial, and competition-driven load spikes may be partly uncontrollable; the author also notes that accepting some risk may be a deliberate performance decision.
paper.practicalImplications: Use rolling averages as compressed descriptions, not athlete-specific injury alarms. Inspect the underlying daily sequence, missing exposures, competition context, and the timing of load before acting. If a decayed or nonlinear model is adopted, validate it prospectively against simpler baselines and report calibration, uncertainty, and decision consequences.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use rolling averages as compressed descriptions, not athlete-specific injury alarms. Inspect the underlying daily sequence, missing exposures, competition context, and the timing of load before acting. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, use rolling averages as compressed descriptions, not athlete-specific injury alarms. Inspect the underlying daily sequence, missing exposures, competition context, and the timing of load before acting. If a decayed or nonlinear model is adopted, validate it prospectively against simpler baselines and report calibration, uncertainty, and decision consequences. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
